questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wire of length 2 m and uniform cross-sectional area 0.5 mm² is made of an alloy of resistivity 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m. Its resistance is:

solution.concept: Resistance from resistivity: R = ρL/A
solution.explanation: Resistance grows with length and falls with area; the material enters only through ρ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.4 Ω takes 0.5 mm² as 5 × 10⁻⁶ m². 2 Ω leaves out the length (ρ/A). 4 × 10⁻³ Ω converts mm² to m² with 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁶.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity of various materials

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform electric field of 0.034 V/m is maintained along a copper wire. The resistivity of copper is 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. The current density in the wire is:

solution.concept: Ohm's law in microscopic form: J = σE = E/ρ
solution.explanation: Current density is proportional to the local electric field; the constant of proportionality is the conductivity σ = 1/ρ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ A/m² multiplies ρ and E. 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ A/m² divides ρ by E. 2.0 × 10⁴ A/m² uses 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ (the value of ρ in Ω cm) as if it were in Ω m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law (J = σE)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 6 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across an ideal 12 V battery. The total power drawn from the battery is:

solution.concept: Power in a parallel combination: P = V²/R for each branch, and the branch powers add
solution.explanation: In parallel each resistor has the full 12 V across it, so each branch dissipates V²/R independently.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 W treats the resistors as being in series (144/9). 24 W and 48 W count only one of the two branches.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy and power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A given metal wire is altered in each of the ways listed below, one at a time. Which change alters the resistivity of the wire?

options.text: Stretching it to twice its length at the same temperature
Cutting it into two equal halves at the same temperature
Passing a larger current through it while keeping its temperature fixed

solution.concept: Resistivity is a property of the material at a given temperature
solution.explanation: Resistance R = ρL/A depends on the shape of the wire, but resistivity ρ depends only on the material and its temperature. For a metal, ρ rises with temperature because the electrons collide more often.
steps: Stretching or cutting changes L and A, so R changes, but ρ does not
At fixed temperature ρ is independent of the current
solution.why_others_wrong: The first three options change the resistance (or nothing at all), not the resistivity of the metal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The potential difference across the terminals of a cell is 1.5 V when no current is drawn from it, and falls to 1.4 V when it supplies a current of 2 A. The internal resistance of the cell is:

solution.concept: Terminal voltage of a discharging cell: V = ε − Ir
solution.explanation: The open-circuit terminal voltage equals the emf. The fall in terminal voltage when current flows is the drop across the internal resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.7 Ω is V/I, the external resistance. 0.75 Ω is ε/I, the total resistance of the circuit. 0.2 Ω multiplies the voltage drop by the current instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Wheatstone bridge, P = 10 Ω and Q = 20 Ω are in series in one branch, and R = 15 Ω and S are in series in the other branch. Both branches are connected across the same cell, with P and R joined at its positive terminal. The galvanometer is connected between the P–Q junction and the R–S junction. The value of S for which the galvanometer shows no deflection is:

solution.concept: Balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge: P/Q = R/S
solution.explanation: At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so the ratios of resistances in the two arms on either side of it are equal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5 Ω uses P/Q = S/R. 25 Ω simply adds P and R. 13.3 Ω takes S = PQ/R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal 12 V battery is connected across two branches in parallel. Branch 1 has a 4 Ω resistor followed by a 2 Ω resistor; branch 2 has a 3 Ω resistor followed by a 6 Ω resistor. In each branch the first-named resistor is joined to the positive terminal. P is the junction of the 4 Ω and 2 Ω resistors and Q is the junction of the 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors. The magnitude of the potential difference between P and Q is:

solution.concept: Potential along each branch of a circuit (Kirchhoff's loop rule)
solution.explanation: Each branch has the full 12 V across it. Find the potential of P and of Q above the negative terminal from the drops along each branch, then subtract.
steps: Branch 1: I = 12/6 = 2 A; drop across 4 Ω = 8 V → V_P = 12 − 8 = 4 V
Branch 2: I = 12/9 = 4/3 A; drop across 3 Ω = 4 V → V_Q = 12 − 4 = 8 V
|V_P − V_Q| = 4 V (Q is at the higher potential)
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 V assumes a balanced bridge, but 4/2 ≠ 3/6. 8 V is the potential of Q above the negative terminal, not the difference between P and Q. 12 V is the full battery voltage.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Wire X has length L and diameter d. Wire Y, made of the same material, has length 2L and diameter 2d. The two wires are connected in parallel across a battery. The ratio of the heat produced per second in X to that in Y is:

solution.concept: Resistance R = ρL/A with A ∝ d², and power in parallel P = V²/R
solution.explanation: First compare the resistances, then use the fact that both wires have the same voltage across them.
steps: R ∝ L/d²: R_X ∝ L/d², R_Y ∝ 2L/(4d²) = (1/2)(L/d²) → R_X = 2R_Y
In parallel, P = V²/R, so P_X/P_Y = R_Y/R_X = 1/2
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 uses P = I²R as if the wires were in series. 1 : 1 assumes the doubled length cancels the doubled diameter (it does not, since area goes as d²). 1 : 4 ignores the doubled length of Y.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity; electrical power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell sends a current of 1.0 A through an external resistance of 4 Ω, and a current of 0.5 A through an external resistance of 9 Ω. The emf and internal resistance of the cell are:

solution.concept: Circuit equation of a cell: ε = I(R + r)
solution.explanation: The emf and internal resistance are the same in both cases, so write ε = I(R + r) twice and solve the pair.
solution.shortcut: Check each option in both equations; only 5 V, 1 Ω gives 1.0 A with 4 Ω and 0.5 A with 9 Ω.
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other pairs gives 1.0 A with 4 Ω but not 0.5 A with 9 Ω: 4.5/9.5 = 0.47 A, 6/11 = 0.55 A, 4/9 = 0.44 A. They come from using only the first reading.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a metre bridge, a resistance X is in the left gap and a standard resistance in the right gap; the null point is 75.0 cm from the left end. X is then shunted by connecting another resistor equal to X in parallel with it, the standard resistance being unchanged. The new null point is at a distance from the left end of:

solution.concept: Metre bridge balance: X/R = l/(100 − l)
solution.explanation: Find X/R from the first balance, halve X (two equal resistors in parallel), and find the new balance length.
solution.why_others_wrong: 37.5 cm halves the balancing length instead of the resistance. 85.7 cm doubles the ratio (X/R = 6) instead of halving it. 40.0 cm is the correct balance measured from the right end.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge (metre bridge)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Around any closed loop of a circuit, the algebraic sum of the changes in potential (across resistors and cells) is zero.
Reason (R): The electrostatic force is conservative, so the net work it does on a charge taken once around a closed path and brought back to its starting point is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's loop rule and its basis
solution.explanation: Potential is a single-valued function of position because the electrostatic field is conservative. A charge that goes round a loop and returns to its starting point is back at the same potential, so the changes in potential around the loop must add to zero. R is the reason for A.
steps: R: zero work round a closed path for a conservative force → true
Zero net work per unit charge = zero net change in potential → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not a separate fact here; it is exactly why the loop rule holds, so option B is wrong. Both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The mobility of conduction electrons, defined as the drift speed per unit electric field, equals eτ/m, where τ is the average time between collisions.
Statement II: In a metallic conductor at a fixed temperature, the drift speed of the electrons is directly proportional to the electric field in the conductor.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Drift velocity, relaxation time and mobility
solution.explanation: An electron accelerated by eE/m for an average time τ acquires an average (drift) velocity v_d = eEτ/m. At a fixed temperature τ is fixed, so v_d ∝ E, and v_d/E = eτ/m is the mobility.
steps: μ = v_d/E = eτ/m → Statement I true
τ constant at fixed temperature → v_d ∝ E → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements follow from v_d = eEτ/m, so any option calling either false is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity; mobility
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Four identical resistors, each of resistance R, are connected in the ways described in List-I. Match each arrangement with its equivalent resistance in List-II.

List-I:
A. All four in series
B. All four in parallel
C. Two in series, and this pair connected in parallel with the other two in series
D. Three in parallel, and this group connected in series with the fourth

List-II:
I. R/4
II. 4R/3
III. 4R
IV. R

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Series and parallel combinations
solution.explanation: Series resistances add; for parallel resistances the reciprocals add.
steps: A: R + R + R + R = 4R → III
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the two mixed arrangements or the series and parallel results.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors (series and parallel)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Twelve identical resistors, each of 6 Ω, form the edges of a cube. The equivalent resistance between two corners of the cube that are at opposite ends of a body diagonal is:

solution.concept: Equivalent resistance using symmetry (equipotential points)
solution.explanation: Feed current I in at one corner and take it out at the opposite corner. By symmetry it splits equally into the three edges at each end and into the six middle edges.
steps: Entry corner: three edges, each carries I/3
Middle: six edges, each carries I/6
Exit corner: three edges, each carries I/3
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.5 Ω (7R/12) is the resistance between the ends of one edge. 4.5 Ω (3R/4) is the resistance across a face diagonal. 72 Ω puts all twelve resistors in series.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal 7 V battery is connected between points A (positive) and C. Between A and C there are two paths: A to B through 1 Ω and then B to C through 2 Ω; and A to D through 2 Ω and then D to C through 1 Ω. Points B and D are joined by a 1 Ω resistor. The current in the resistor joining B and D is:

options.text: 1 A, flowing from B to D
1 A, flowing from D to B
zero, since the bridge is balanced
5 A, flowing from B to D

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's rules (node potentials) for an unbalanced bridge
solution.explanation: Take C as zero potential and A at 7 V. Write the junction rule at B and at D for the unknown potentials, solve, and find the current from the potential difference across BD.
steps: I(BD) = (4 − 3)/1 = 1 A, from B (higher potential) to D
solution.why_others_wrong: The bridge is not balanced (1/2 ≠ 2/1), so the current is not zero. B is at the higher potential, so the current is not from D to B. 5 A is the total current drawn from the battery, not the current in BD.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules; Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option A: 1 A, flowing from B to D

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A wire whose cross-section is not uniform carries a steady current; the drift speed of its free electrons is greater in the thinner parts of the wire.
Statement II: In such a wire, the electric field inside the wire has the same magnitude at every cross-section.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Steady current through a non-uniform conductor: I = neAv_d and J = σE
solution.explanation: In steady state the same current I passes every cross-section. With the same n everywhere, v_d = I/(neA) is larger where A is smaller. The current density J = I/A is also larger there, and since E = J/σ = ρJ, the field is larger in the thinner parts too.
steps: Same I at every section (charge does not pile up)
v_d = I/(neA) ∝ 1/A → larger where thinner → I true
E = ρI/A ∝ 1/A → not the same everywhere → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II would hold only for a uniform wire. Statement I is true, so options calling it false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons; resistivity (J = σE)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A cell of emf ε and internal resistance r is connected across an external resistor whose resistance R can be varied from zero upwards. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The current is largest when R = 0, and then equals ε/r.
(b) When R = r, the cell delivers 100% of the power it generates to the external resistor.
(c) The potential difference across the terminals of the cell increases as R is increased.
(d) As R is increased beyond r, the power dissipated in the external resistor keeps increasing.
(e) The power dissipated in the external resistor is greatest when R = r.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Current, terminal voltage and power for a cell with internal resistance
solution.explanation: I = ε/(R + r), V = IR = εR/(R + r) and P = ε²R/(R + r)². P is greatest when R = r, where the efficiency R/(R + r) is only 50%; beyond R = r the power falls again.
steps: (a) R = 0 → I = ε/r, the largest value → true
(b) efficiency = R/(R + r) = 1/2 at R = r → 50%, not 100% → false
(c) V = ε/(1 + r/R) increases with R → true
(d) P decreases for R > r → false
(e) dP/dR = 0 at R = r → maximum → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing (b) or (d) is wrong, and any option missing one of (a), (c), (e) is incomplete.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance; electrical power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about Ohm's law and its limitations are correct?

(a) For a p-n junction diode, reversing the direction of an applied voltage of the same magnitude does not give a current of the same magnitude in the opposite direction.
(b) For a material such as GaAs, the same current can flow at more than one value of the applied voltage.
(c) At constant temperature, the graph of current against voltage for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin.
(d) The resistance of an ohmic conductor kept at constant temperature changes with the current through it.
(e) A device whose current depends on the sign of the applied voltage obeys Ohm's law.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ohmic and non-ohmic behaviour
solution.explanation: Ohm's law (V ∝ I with constant R at fixed temperature) is not universal. NCERT lists three kinds of departure: V stops being proportional to I, the relation depends on the sign of V (as in a diode), and the relation is not unique (as in GaAs).
steps: (a) diode: depends on sign of V → true
(b) GaAs: V–I relation not unique → true
(c) ohmic conductor: straight line through origin → true
(d) ohmic means R constant at fixed temperature → false
(e) a sign-dependent device is non-ohmic → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) or (e) include a false statement; they confuse the definition of an ohmic conductor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', limitations of Ohm's law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A flat circular coil of 50 turns and radius 10 cm carries a current of 2 A. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic field at the centre of the coil is:

solution.concept: Field at the centre of a circular coil: B = µ₀NI/(2R)
solution.explanation: Each turn contributes µ₀I/(2R) at the centre (from the Biot-Savart law), and the N turns add.
solution.why_others_wrong: π × 10⁻⁴ T uses µ₀NI/(4R), the result for a semicircle. 4π × 10⁻⁴ T drops the 2 in the denominator. 4π × 10⁻⁶ T ignores the number of turns.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A straight wire 0.5 m long carries a current of 4 A in a uniform magnetic field of 0.3 T. The wire makes an angle of 30° with the direction of the field. The magnitude of the magnetic force on the wire is:

solution.concept: Force on a current-carrying conductor: F = BIL sin θ
solution.explanation: Only the component of the field perpendicular to the wire exerts a force on it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.52 N uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°. 0.60 N takes the wire to be perpendicular to the field. 0.15 N halves the answer a second time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: An electron (mass 9 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves with a speed of 1.6 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 9 × 10⁻⁵ T. The radius of its circular path is:

solution.concept: Circular motion in a magnetic field: r = mv/(qB)
solution.explanation: The magnetic force qvB supplies the centripetal force mv²/r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm and 5 cm come from an extra factor of 2 in the numerator or the denominator. 62.8 cm is the circumference 2πr, not the radius.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: According to Ampere's circuital law, the line integral of the magnetic field B around any closed path is equal to µ₀ times:

options.text: the total current in all conductors near the path, whether or not they pass through it
the net current passing through the surface bounded by the closed path
the current per unit length of the path

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law: ∮B·dl = µ₀I_enclosed
solution.explanation: Only currents that thread the closed loop (pass through a surface bounded by it) contribute to the line integral. Currents outside the loop change B at points on the loop but add nothing to the integral.
steps: ∮B·dl = µ₀ I_e, where I_e is the net current through the surface bounded by the loop
solution.why_others_wrong: Currents outside the loop do not count. 'Current per unit length' and 'zero always' do not state the law.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law
solution.final_answer: Option B: the net current passing through the surface bounded by the closed path

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: When a ferromagnetic material is heated above a certain temperature (its Curie temperature), it becomes:

solution.concept: Temperature dependence of ferromagnetism
solution.explanation: Thermal agitation destroys the alignment of the atomic moments within domains. Above the Curie temperature the ferromagnetic property is lost and the material behaves as a paramagnet.
steps: Above the Curie temperature T_c, the substance is paramagnetic
solution.why_others_wrong: The material does not become diamagnetic or superconducting, and heating weakens rather than strengthens ferromagnetism.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', ferromagnetism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II. (m is a magnetic dipole moment and B a uniform magnetic field.)

List-I:
A. Magnetic moment of a coil of N turns, each of area A, carrying current I
B. Torque on a magnetic dipole m in a uniform field B
C. Potential energy of a magnetic dipole m in a uniform field B
D. Magnetic field at a far axial point, distance r from the centre of a short bar magnet

List-II:
I. m × B
II. NIA
III. µ₀(2m)/(4πr³)
IV. −m·B

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: The current loop and the bar magnet as magnetic dipoles
solution.explanation: A current loop behaves as a dipole of moment m = NIA. In a uniform field a dipole feels a torque m × B and has potential energy −m·B. Far along its axis a short magnet produces B = µ₀(2m)/(4πr³).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap torque with potential energy, or the moment with the torque, or the axial field with the potential energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the magnetic dipole moment of a current loop; 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For an ideal toroid with n turns per unit length carrying a current I, the magnetic field at a point in the open space enclosed by the toroid (not within its windings) is µ₀nI.
Reason (R): A circular Amperian loop drawn through that open space, coaxial with the toroid, encloses no net current.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ampere's law applied to a toroid
solution.explanation: A loop in the open space inside the toroid does not pass through any winding, so the enclosed current is zero and B there is zero. The field µ₀nI exists only in the region enclosed by the windings (the core). A is false and R is true.
steps: Loop in the open space: I_enclosed = 0 → B(2πr) = 0 → B = 0
So A is false; R is true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C (which all need A to be true) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the solenoid and the toroid (Ampere's law)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two identical circular coils, each of one turn and radius 2π cm, have a common centre and their planes are perpendicular to each other. Each carries a current of 1 A. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at the common centre is:

solution.concept: Superposition of magnetic fields (vector addition)
solution.explanation: Each coil gives a field µ₀I/(2R) along its own axis. The two axes are perpendicular, so the fields add as perpendicular vectors.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 × 10⁻⁵ T adds the fields as if they were parallel. Zero assumes they cancel. 1 × 10⁻⁵ T is the field of one coil only.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A wire bent into a semicircle of radius 10 cm carries a current of 5 A. It lies in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The magnitude of the net magnetic force on the semicircular wire is:

solution.concept: Force on a curved wire in a uniform field equals the force on the straight wire joining its ends
solution.explanation: In a uniform field, F = I(∫dl) × B, and ∫dl along any path is the straight vector from one end to the other. For a semicircle this is the diameter 2R, which is perpendicular to B.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.31 N uses the arc length πR as if the arc were straight. 0.10 N uses R instead of 2R. Zero would be correct only for a closed loop.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton (mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T with a speed of 2 × 10⁶ m/s. The time it takes to complete one revolution is:

solution.concept: Period of circular motion in a magnetic field: T = 2πm/(qB), independent of speed
solution.explanation: r = mv/(qB) grows in proportion to v, so the time 2πr/v does not depend on the speed. The speed in the stem is not needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2π × 10⁻⁸ s is the time for half a revolution (πm/qB). 2 × 10⁻⁸ s leaves out the factor 2π. 8π × 10⁻⁸ s doubles the mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a moving-coil galvanometer, the steady deflection of the coil is proportional to the current through it.
Reason (R): The cylindrical pole pieces and the soft-iron core make the magnetic field radial, so the plane of the coil stays parallel to the field and the deflecting torque is NIAB in every position of the coil.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Moving-coil galvanometer: radial field and linear scale
solution.explanation: In equilibrium the deflecting torque balances the spring's restoring torque: NIAB = kφ, so φ = (NAB/k)I. This linear relation needs the torque to be NIAB whatever the angle, which is exactly what the radial field ensures. R explains A.
steps: Radial field → torque = NIAB (no sin θ factor)
solution.why_others_wrong: Without a radial field the torque would vary as sin θ and the deflection would not be proportional to I, so R is the explanation, not an unrelated fact (B is wrong). Both are true (C, D wrong).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Diamagnetism is present in all substances, but in most paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances it is masked by their much stronger paramagnetic or ferromagnetic behaviour.
Statement II: The relative permeability of a diamagnetic substance is slightly less than 1.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Diamagnetism and relative permeability
solution.explanation: Diamagnetism arises from the orbital motion of electrons responding to an applied field, so every substance has it; it is weak and is usually swamped when the atoms have permanent moments. For a diamagnet χ is small and negative, so µr = 1 + χ is slightly less than 1.
steps: Statement I: as stated in NCERT → true
µr = 1 + χ with −1 < χ < 0 (small) → slightly below 1 → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so every other option is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', diamagnetism
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A steady current I flows in each configuration of List-I. Match the configuration with the magnitude of the magnetic field it produces at the stated point (List-II).

List-I:
A. At the centre of a circular loop of radius R
B. At a distance R from a very long straight wire
C. Well inside a long solenoid having n turns per unit length
D. On the axis of a circular loop of radius R, at a distance x from its centre

List-II:
I. µ₀nI
II. µ₀I/(2πR)
III. µ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)]
IV. µ₀I/(2R)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Standard magnetic field results
solution.explanation: These follow from the Biot-Savart law (loop, straight wire) and Ampere's law (solenoid).
steps: Loop axis: µ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)] → III (it reduces to IV at x = 0)
solution.why_others_wrong: The commonest slip is swapping µ₀I/(2R) and µ₀I/(2πR), which differ only by π.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Biot-Savart law applications; Ampere's circuital law
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A circular loop of radius R carries a steady current. The ratio of the magnetic field at a point on its axis at a distance √3 R from its centre to the magnetic field at the centre of the loop is:

solution.concept: Field on the axis of a circular loop: B(x) = µ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)]
solution.explanation: Divide the axial field by the centre field µ₀I/(2R); everything except the geometry cancels.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 forgets the power 3/2 and uses R²/(R² + x²). 1/2 treats the field as falling like 1/x. √3/8 keeps an extra factor of x/R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two long parallel wires P and Q, 30 cm apart, carry currents of 2 A and 8 A respectively in the same direction. A third long straight wire carrying a current is placed parallel to them, in their plane. It experiences no net magnetic force when it is placed:

options.text: between the wires, 24 cm from P
on the far side of P from Q, 10 cm from P
between the wires, 6 cm from P

solution.concept: Force between parallel currents: F/L = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)
solution.explanation: The force on the third wire from each of P and Q is proportional to (that wire's current)/(distance). For no net force the two must be equal and opposite. With P and Q in the same direction, the two forces oppose only between the wires. The result does not depend on the current in the third wire.
steps: Between the wires, at x from P: 2/x = 8/(30 − x)
2(30 − x) = 8x → x = 6 cm from P (nearer the smaller current)
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 cm from P puts the wire nearer the larger current (ratio inverted). 10 cm on the far side of P is where the forces would cancel if the currents were opposite. The midpoint would need equal currents.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', force between two parallel currents
solution.final_answer: Option C: between the wires, 6 cm from P

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A current loop of magnetic moment 0.5 A m² is in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T, its moment making an angle of 60° with the field. The work that must be done by an external agent to turn it slowly until its moment is antiparallel to the field is:

solution.concept: Potential energy of a magnetic dipole: U = −mB cos θ; work done = U_final − U_initial
solution.explanation: Turning the dipole slowly, the external work equals the increase in potential energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.10 J is the work to turn from 0° to 60°. 0.20 J is just mB. 0.40 J (2mB) is the work to turn from 0° to 180°, not from 60°.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the dipole in a uniform magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton moving at right angles to the boundary enters a region of uniform magnetic field directed perpendicular to its velocity. The field region has a width d along the proton's original direction of motion, and the radius of the proton's circular path inside the field is 2d. The angle through which the proton has been deflected when it leaves the field region is:

solution.concept: Circular arc of a charged particle crossing a field region
solution.explanation: Inside the field the proton moves on a circle of radius r whose centre lies on the boundary line through the entry point. After turning through angle θ its displacement along the original direction is r sin θ. It leaves when this equals d (possible because d < r).
solution.why_others_wrong: 60° uses cos θ = d/r. 26.6° uses tan θ = d/r. 90° would need d = r; here d < r, so the proton leaves before turning through a quarter circle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A closed wire loop consists of a semicircle of radius R and a semicircle of radius 2R with a common centre O, joined at their ends by two straight radial segments lying along a diameter. A steady current I flows round the loop. The magnitude of the magnetic field at O is:

solution.concept: Field of a circular arc at its centre: B = (µ₀I/4πR) × (angle subtended); straight segments through O give zero
solution.explanation: Each semicircle gives µ₀I/(4r) at O. Going round the closed loop, the current flows in opposite senses (one clockwise, one anticlockwise about O) in the two arcs, so their fields at O are opposite. The radial segments point at O and contribute nothing.
steps: Outer arc: µ₀I/(4 × 2R) = µ₀I/(8R), opposite in direction
Net B = µ₀I/(4R) − µ₀I/(8R) = µ₀I/(8R), in the direction of the inner arc's field
solution.why_others_wrong: 3µ₀I/(8R) adds the two fields although the current goes round O in opposite senses. µ₀I/(4R) counts only the inner arc. Zero would need equal radii.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a current element, Biot-Savart law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about magnetic materials are correct?

(a) The relative permeability of a ferromagnetic material is much greater than 1.
(b) When a diamagnetic material is placed in an external magnetic field, the field lines are pushed out of it and the field inside the material is reduced.
(c) In a ferromagnetic material, the magnetisation produced is opposite to the applied magnetic field.
(d) Copper and water are paramagnetic substances.
(e) Aluminium, sodium and calcium are paramagnetic substances.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Classification of magnetic materials
solution.explanation: Ferromagnets: µr ≫ 1, magnetisation along the field. Diamagnets: field lines expelled, B inside reduced, χ < 0. NCERT lists copper, water, bismuth and lead among diamagnetic substances, and aluminium, sodium, calcium and oxygen (at STP) among paramagnetic ones.
steps: (c) false: magnetisation is along the field (only a diamagnet opposes it)
(d) false: copper and water are diamagnetic
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (d) include a false statement; the remaining option leaves out (e) or another true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetic properties of materials

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current in a coil of self-inductance 0.3 H falls steadily from 6 A to 2 A in 0.1 s. The magnitude of the emf induced in the coil is:

solution.concept: Self-induced emf: ε = −L dI/dt
solution.explanation: A changing current changes the coil's own flux (NΦ = LI), which induces an emf opposing the change.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 V uses the initial current (6 A) instead of the change. 24 V adds the two currents. 1.2 V forgets to divide by the time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A capacitor of capacitance (50/π) µF is connected to a 50 Hz AC supply. Its capacitive reactance is:

solution.concept: Capacitive reactance: X_C = 1/(ωC) = 1/(2πfC)
solution.explanation: A capacitor offers less opposition at higher frequency; its reactance falls as 1/f.
solution.why_others_wrong: 400π Ω uses 1/(fC), leaving out 2π. 5 × 10⁻³ Ω is ωC, not its reciprocal. 2 × 10⁵ Ω reads the capacitance as (50/π) nF.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a capacitor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The north pole of a bar magnet is moved towards one face of a closed circular coil. As seen from the side of the approaching magnet, the current induced in the coil flows:

options.text: anticlockwise, so that this face of the coil behaves as a north pole
clockwise, so that this face of the coil behaves as a south pole
nowhere, because the coil is not connected to any battery
clockwise, so that this face of the coil behaves as a north pole

solution.concept: Lenz's law
solution.explanation: The induced current opposes the change that causes it. The approaching north pole increases the flux, so the facing side of the coil becomes a north pole to repel it. A current that looks anticlockwise from that side makes that face a north pole.
steps: Flux towards the coil increases → induced current must oppose the approach
Facing side becomes N → current anticlockwise as seen by the magnet
solution.why_others_wrong: A south-pole face would attract the magnet and help the change, against Lenz's law. A closed coil needs no battery for an induced current. A clockwise current makes the facing side a south pole, not a north pole.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law and conservation of energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: anticlockwise, so that this face of the coil behaves as a north pole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each situation in List-I with the expression for the induced emf in List-II.

List-I:
A. Emf in a coil of N turns linked by a changing magnetic flux Φ_B
B. Emf across a rod of length l moving with speed v perpendicular to a uniform field B
C. Peak emf of an AC generator with N turns of area A rotating at angular speed ω in field B
D. Emf induced in coil 2 when the current I₁ in a neighbouring coil 1 changes

List-II:
I. NBAω
II. −N dΦ_B/dt
III. −M dI₁/dt
IV. Bvl

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Faraday's law and its applications
solution.explanation: All four follow from ε = −dΦ/dt applied to different set-ups.
steps: A: Faraday's law for N turns → II
C: ε = NBAω sin ωt, peak NBAω → I
D: mutual induction, ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt → III
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the motional emf with the generator emf, or the mutual-induction emf with Faraday's law in general.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law; motional emf; mutual inductance; 'Alternating Current' (AC generator)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal rod of length 0.4 m rotates with an angular speed of 20 rad/s about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod. A uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T is parallel to the axis of rotation. The emf induced between the ends of the rod is:

solution.concept: Motional emf in a rotating rod: ε = ½BωL²
solution.explanation: Different parts of the rod move with different speeds v = ωr. Adding the small emfs B(ωr)dr from r = 0 to L gives ½BωL² (equivalently, B × the average speed ωL/2 × L).
solution.shortcut: Use the speed of the midpoint: v_avg = ωL/2 = 4 m/s, so ε = B v_avg L = 0.5 × 4 × 0.4 = 0.8 V.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.6 V leaves out the ½ (uses the speed of the free end for the whole rod). 4.0 V uses BωL, which is not even dimensionally an emf. 0.4 V puts in an extra factor ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An air-cored solenoid is 50 cm long, has 500 turns and a cross-sectional area of 10 cm². Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, its self-inductance is about:

solution.concept: Self-inductance of a long solenoid: L = µ₀N²A/l
solution.explanation: The field µ₀(N/l)I links all N turns of area A, so NΦ = µ₀N²AI/l and L = NΦ/I.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.3 µH uses N instead of N². 6.3 mH takes 10 cm² as 10⁻² m². 0.31 mH divides by 2l.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A series circuit of a 40 Ω resistor, an inductor of reactance 50 Ω and a capacitor of reactance 20 Ω is connected to a 220 V (rms) AC supply. The rms current and its phase relative to the supply voltage are:

solution.concept: Impedance of a series LCR circuit: Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²]
solution.explanation: The net reactance is X_L − X_C. Since it is positive (inductive), the current lags the voltage.
steps: X_L > X_C → circuit is inductive → current lags (tan φ = 30/40, φ ≈ 37°)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Leading' would need X_C > X_L. 2.0 A adds R, X_L and X_C arithmetically. 7.3 A uses only the net reactance and ignores R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a series LCR circuit
solution.final_answer: Option B: 4.4 A, lagging the voltage

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit with R = 10 Ω is connected to an AC source of rms voltage 20 V whose frequency is set so that the circuit is in resonance; at this frequency the inductive reactance is 100 Ω. The rms voltage across the inductor is:

solution.concept: Series resonance: X_L = X_C, Z = R; voltages across L and C are equal and opposite
solution.explanation: At resonance the impedance is just R, so the current is large; the voltage across L (and across C) is I·X_L, which can be many times the source voltage. The two cancel each other in the loop.
steps: At resonance Z = R = 10 Ω → I = 20/10 = 2 A
V_L = I X_L = 2 × 100 = 200 V (and V_C = 200 V, opposite in phase)
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 V assumes no element can have more voltage than the source. Zero is the sum V_L + V_C, not V_L. 10 V halves the source voltage for no reason.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', resonance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): An ideal inductor connected to an AC source consumes no power on average over a complete cycle.
Reason (R): In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current is in phase with the applied voltage.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Power in a purely inductive circuit
solution.explanation: In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by π/2, so the power factor cos φ = 0 and the average power V I cos φ = 0. Energy taken in one quarter cycle is returned in the next. A is true; R is false.
steps: φ = π/2 for a pure inductor
P_avg = V_rms I_rms cos(π/2) = 0 → A true
Current lags by π/2, not in phase → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so options A, B and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to an inductor; power in AC circuit
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about inductance are correct?

(a) The self-inductance of a coil depends on its geometry and on the permeability of the medium inside it, not on the current through it.
(b) Inserting a soft-iron core into a coil increases its self-inductance.
(c) A self-induced emf always opposes the current in the coil.
(d) For a pair of coils, the mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2 equals that of coil 2 with respect to coil 1.
(e) The SI unit of self-inductance is the tesla.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Self and mutual inductance
solution.explanation: L = µ₀µr N²A/l depends on geometry and the core. The induced emf opposes the change in current (it can be along the current when the current is falling). M₁₂ = M₂₁. The unit of inductance is the henry.
steps: (c) false: it opposes the change of current, not the current itself
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (e) include a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance (mutual and self)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A coil of 100 turns, each of area 100 cm², has a total resistance of 5 Ω and its ends are joined. It lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. It is then turned over through 180° about a diameter. The total charge that flows round the coil during the turn is:

solution.concept: Charge induced by a flux change: Q = NΔΦ/R
solution.explanation: I = ε/R = −(N/R)dΦ/dt, so the charge Q = ∫I dt = NΔΦ/R depends only on the total change in flux, not on how fast the coil is turned. Turning over reverses the flux through each turn.
steps: A = 100 cm² = 0.01 m²; Φ changes from +BA to −BA
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 C takes the flux change as BA, as for turning through 90°. Zero assumes the flux is the same because its magnitude is unchanged, but its sign reverses. 1.0 C forgets to divide by the resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 100 Ω resistor and an inductor of inductance (1/π) H are connected in series to a 200 V (rms), 50 Hz supply. A capacitor is to be added in series so that the power factor of the circuit becomes 1. The capacitance needed and the power then drawn from the supply are:

solution.concept: Power-factor correction: make X_C = X_L (series resonance); then P = V²/R
solution.explanation: A power factor of 1 means the net reactance is zero, so the capacitor must cancel the inductive reactance. The impedance then equals R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 W is the power before the capacitor is added (Z = 100√2 Ω, I = √2 A). (200/π) µF gives X_C = 50 Ω and (50/π) µF gives X_C = 200 Ω; neither cancels X_L.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', resonance; power in AC circuit: the power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In an AC generator, the emf induced in the rotating coil is greatest at the instant when the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field.
Statement II: The average value of a sinusoidal alternating current over one complete cycle is equal to its rms value.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: AC generator emf and average versus rms values
solution.explanation: With Φ = NBA cos ωt, the emf is NBAω sin ωt. It is largest when ωt = 90°, when the flux through the coil is zero, i.e. when the plane of the coil is parallel to B (the flux is then changing fastest). The average of a sinusoid over a full cycle is zero, while its rms value is I₀/√2.
steps: ε = NBAω sin ωt; maximum when the coil's plane ∥ B → Statement I true
Average over a cycle = 0 ≠ I₀/√2 → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Many students think the emf is greatest when the flux is greatest; it is the rate of change of flux that matters. Statement II is false, so options A and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction'/'Alternating Current', AC generator; rms value
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A series LCR circuit (with R ≠ 0) is driven by an AC source whose frequency is below the resonant frequency of the circuit. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The capacitive reactance is greater than the inductive reactance.
(b) The current leads the applied voltage.
(c) The power factor of the circuit is less than 1.
(d) Increasing the capacitance, with L, R and the source frequency unchanged, takes the circuit further away from resonance.
(e) The impedance of the circuit is less than R.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Behaviour of a series LCR circuit off resonance
solution.explanation: Below resonance, ω < 1/√(LC), so ωL < 1/(ωC): the circuit is capacitive and the current leads. The impedance √[R² + (X_C − X_L)²] exceeds R and cos φ = R/Z < 1. Increasing C lowers the resonant frequency 1/√(LC) towards the source frequency, bringing the circuit closer to resonance.
steps: (d) larger C → smaller ω₀ → closer to ω → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit; resonance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Special vacuum tubes called klystrons and magnetrons, and Gunn diodes, are used to produce:

solution.concept: Production of the different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that microwaves (used in radar and microwave ovens) are produced by klystrons, magnetrons and Gunn diodes. Radio waves come from accelerated charges in conducting wires (antennas), infrared from hot bodies, and X-rays from bombarding a metal target with high-energy electrons.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other radiations have different sources, listed in the explanation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum (microwaves)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The electric field of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is E_y = E₀ sin(200πx − 6π × 10¹⁰ t), with x in metres and t in seconds. The wavelength of the wave and the part of the spectrum it belongs to are:

solution.concept: Plane wave E = E₀ sin(kx − ωt): λ = 2π/k, f = ω/2π, v = ω/k
solution.explanation: Read k and ω from the phase. A check that ω/k = 3 × 10⁸ m/s confirms the wave is in vacuum.
steps: ω = 6π × 10¹⁰ rad/s → f = 3 × 10¹⁰ Hz; ω/k = 3 × 10⁸ m/s ✓
Microwaves span about 1 mm to 0.1 m → 1 cm is a microwave
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 cm uses λ = π/k. 'Infrared' mis-places 1 cm; infrared lies between about 1 mm and 700 nm. 100 m reads k/(2π) = 100 as the wavelength.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves; electromagnetic spectrum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): An electromagnetic wave falling on a surface exerts a pressure on it.
Reason (R): Electromagnetic waves carry energy but do not carry momentum.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Momentum and radiation pressure of electromagnetic waves
solution.explanation: An electromagnetic wave carries momentum as well as energy: a wave delivering energy U to a surface that absorbs it completely delivers momentum U/c. The momentum delivered per second per unit area is the radiation pressure. A is true; R is false.
steps: EM waves carry momentum p = U/c → R false
Momentum transfer to the surface → force → pressure → A true
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so options A, B and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (momentum and radiation pressure)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A parallel-plate capacitor with circular plates of radius 10 cm is being charged by a steady current of 2 A. Neglecting edge effects and taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the magnetic field between the plates at a distance of 5 cm from their common axis is:

options.text: zero, since no conduction current flows between the plates

solution.concept: Ampere-Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀(i_c + i_d); displacement current i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt
solution.explanation: Between the plates the displacement current equals the charging current, spread uniformly over the plate area. A circular loop of radius r encloses the fraction r²/R² of it.
steps: i_d (total) = 2 A; enclosed by loop of radius r: 2 × (5/10)² = 0.5 A
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero ignores the displacement current. 8 × 10⁻⁶ T treats the full 2 A as enclosed within r = 5 cm. 4 × 10⁻⁶ T is the field at the edge of the plates (r = 10 cm).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm. The image is formed:

options.text: 10 cm in front of the mirror; magnification −0.5

solution.concept: Mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with m = −v/u (Cartesian sign convention)
solution.explanation: For a convex mirror f is positive (focus behind the mirror) and a real object has negative u.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'At infinity' is the answer for a concave mirror with the object at its focus. '20 cm behind, +1' treats the mirror as plane. '10 cm in front, −0.5' gets the size right but takes the image as real (sign slip).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', the mirror equation
solution.final_answer: Option B: 10 cm behind the mirror; magnification +0.5

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 600 nm in vacuum enters a glass block of refractive index 1.5. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the wavelength and the frequency of the light inside the glass are:

solution.concept: On refraction, frequency is unchanged; speed and wavelength are divided by n
solution.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source. Since v = c/n and v = fλ, the wavelength in the medium is λ₀/n.
solution.why_others_wrong: 900 nm multiplies by n instead of dividing. 3.3 × 10¹⁴ Hz wrongly reduces the frequency by n. 600 nm and 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz keep the wavelength and change the frequency, the reverse of what happens.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction; 'Wave Optics', refraction of a plane wave

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin plano-convex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.5, and the radius of curvature of its curved surface is 20 cm. Its focal length in air is:

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
solution.explanation: For the plane surface 1/R = 0, so only the curved surface contributes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm is the focal length of an equiconvex lens with both radii 20 cm. 13.3 cm uses n instead of (n − 1). 10 cm multiplies R by (n − 1) instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens: lens maker's formula

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An optical fibre consists of a central core surrounded by a cladding. Light launched into the core is guided along the fibre, even round bends, because:

options.text: the refractive index of the core is greater than that of the cladding
the refractive index of the cladding is greater than that of the core
the core and the cladding have the same refractive index
the boundary between the core and the cladding is silvered like a mirror

solution.concept: Optical fibres and total internal reflection
solution.explanation: Total internal reflection needs light to go from a denser to a rarer medium at more than the critical angle. Making the core optically denser than the cladding lets light striking the core–cladding boundary at large angles be totally reflected again and again.
steps: Rays meeting the boundary above the critical angle are trapped in the core
solution.why_others_wrong: A denser cladding or equal indices make TIR at the boundary impossible. The fibre is not silvered; reflection is total because of refraction physics, not a metal coating.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection (optical fibres)
solution.final_answer: Option A: the refractive index of the core is greater than that of the cladding

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: According to Huygens' principle:

options.text: each point on a wavefront absorbs the light falling on it and re-emits it only in the backward direction
only the centre of a wavefront acts as a source of new waves
a wavefront is a surface on which the disturbance has different phases at different points
each point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, and the forward envelope of these wavelets gives the position of the wavefront at a later time

solution.concept: Huygens' construction of wavefronts
solution.explanation: A wavefront is a surface of constant phase. Every point on it acts as a source of secondary wavelets moving with the wave speed; the common tangent (envelope) to these wavelets in the forward direction is the new wavefront. Huygens assumed the backwave to be absent.
steps: Wavefront: locus of points in the same phase
New wavefront = forward envelope of secondary wavelets
solution.why_others_wrong: The backward-only and 'centre only' versions misstate the principle, and a wavefront is a surface of the same phase, not of different phases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', Huygens principle
solution.final_answer: Option D: each point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, and the forward envelope of these wavelets gives the position of the wavefront at a later time

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. In normal adjustment (final image at infinity), the magnifying power and the distance between the two lenses are:

solution.concept: Telescope in normal adjustment: m = f_o/f_e, L = f_o + f_e
solution.explanation: The objective forms the image of a distant object at its focus; for a final image at infinity this point must also be the focus of the eyepiece.
solution.why_others_wrong: 95 cm subtracts the focal lengths. 0.05 is f_e/f_o, the ratio upside down. 500 multiplies the focal lengths.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments: telescope

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
An object is placed on the principal axis of a concave mirror (C = centre of curvature, F = focus, P = pole). Match the position of the object (List-I) with the nature and position of the image (List-II).

List-I:
A. Beyond C
B. At F
C. Between F and C
D. Between P and F

List-II:
I. Virtual, erect, magnified, behind the mirror
II. Real, inverted, highly magnified, at infinity
III. Real, inverted, magnified, beyond C
IV. Real, inverted, diminished, between F and C

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Image formation by a concave mirror
solution.explanation: Use 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, or ray diagrams, for each object position.
steps: Beyond C → image between F and C, real, inverted, diminished (IV)
Between F and C → image beyond C, real, inverted, magnified (III)
Between P and F → virtual, erect, magnified, behind the mirror (I)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the images for objects beyond C and between F and C (they are interchangeable by reversibility of light), or the images for objects at F and inside F.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a thin convex lens of focal length 15 cm. The image formed is:

options.text: 6 cm from the lens on the other side; real, inverted and 0.6 times the size of the object
30 cm from the lens on the other side; real, inverted and 3 times the size of the object
30 cm from the lens on the same side as the object; virtual, erect and 1/3 the size of the object
30 cm from the lens on the same side as the object; virtual, erect and 3 times the size of the object

solution.concept: Thin lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f and magnification m = v/u
solution.explanation: An object inside the focal length of a convex lens gives a virtual, erect, magnified image on the same side (the lens acts as a magnifier).
steps: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/15 − 1/10 = −1/30 → v = −30 cm (same side as the object)
m = v/u = (−30)/(−10) = +3 → virtual, erect, magnified 3 times
solution.why_others_wrong: '6 cm, other side' adds 1/15 and 1/10 (sign of u dropped). '30 cm on the other side, real' ignores the sign of v. '1/3 the size' takes m = u/v.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', thin lens formula; magnification
solution.final_answer: Option D: 30 cm from the lens on the same side as the object; virtual, erect and 3 times the size of the object

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin prism of refracting angle 5° made of glass of refractive index 1.6 is combined with a second thin prism of glass of refractive index 1.5, placed the other way round, so that a ray passing through both suffers no net deviation. The refracting angle of the second prism is:

solution.concept: Deviation by a thin prism: δ = (n − 1)A
solution.explanation: The inverted second prism deviates the ray the opposite way; for zero net deviation its deviation must equal that of the first.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.17° inverts the ratio of (n − 1) values. 5.33° uses the ratio of n instead of (n − 1). 3° is the deviation of the first prism, not the angle of the second.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism (thin prism)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment the slits are 1 mm apart, the screen is 1 m away and light of wavelength 600 nm is used. The distance between the second dark fringe and the fifth bright fringe, both on the same side of the central bright fringe, is:

solution.concept: Fringe positions in YDSE: bright y = nβ, dark y = (n − ½)β, with β = λD/d
solution.explanation: Count fringes in units of β from the central bright fringe. The first dark fringe is at β/2, the second at 3β/2.
steps: Fifth bright: 5β = 3.0 mm; second dark: 1.5β = 0.9 mm
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 mm places the second dark fringe at 2.5β. 1.8 mm places it at 2β, as if it were a bright fringe. 3.0 mm is the distance of the fifth bright fringe from the centre.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Unpolarised light falls on a plane glass surface (refractive index √3) at the angle of incidence for which the reflected light is completely plane polarised. The angle of refraction is:

solution.concept: Brewster's law: tan i_B = n
solution.explanation: At the Brewster angle the reflected light is completely polarised. Find i_B from tan i_B = n and then the refraction angle from Snell's law.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60° is the angle of incidence, not of refraction. 35.3° is sin⁻¹(1/√3), the critical angle. 45° has no basis here.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation by reflection

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For a Young's double-slit experiment (slit separation d, screen distance D, wavelength λ) and a single-slit diffraction experiment (slit width a), match List-I with List-II.

List-I:
A. Fringe width in Young's experiment
B. Distance of the nth bright fringe from the central bright fringe
C. Path difference at the nth dark fringe (n = 1, 2, 3, ...)
D. Angular position of the first minimum of the single-slit pattern (small angles)

List-II:
I. (n − ½)λ
II. λ/a
III. nλD/d
IV. λD/d

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Interference and diffraction formulae
solution.explanation: In YDSE, bright fringes are at y = nλD/d (path difference nλ) and dark fringes at path difference (n − ½)λ; the spacing is λD/d. For a single slit, the first minimum is at sin θ = λ/a.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the fringe width with the fringe position, or the dark-fringe condition with the single-slit minimum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference; diffraction at a single slit
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Objectives of large diameter are used in astronomical telescopes.
Reason (R): A larger objective collects more light, so fainter objects can be seen, and it also gives a better resolving power.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Light-gathering power and resolution of a telescope
solution.explanation: The light-gathering power depends on the area of the objective, and the ability to see two close objects separately (resolving power) also improves with the diameter of the objective. These two advantages are why large objectives are used. R explains A.
steps: Both are reasons for large objectives
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the very reasons for A, so B is wrong. Both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', telescope
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The focal length of a spherical mirror changes when the mirror is immersed in water.
Statement II: A spherical mirror forms images free of chromatic aberration because its focal length does not depend on the wavelength of light.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Focal length of a mirror: f = R/2
solution.explanation: A mirror works by reflection, and the law of reflection does not involve the refractive index of the medium or the wavelength. So f = R/2 is the same in water as in air, and the same for all colours, which is one advantage of reflecting telescopes.
steps: f = R/2: depends only on the geometry → I false
No dependence on λ → no chromatic aberration → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false (it would be true for a lens). Statement II is true, so B and C are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', spherical mirrors; reflecting telescope
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about optical instruments are correct?

(a) In an astronomical telescope, the focal length of the objective is smaller than that of the eyepiece.
(b) In a compound microscope, both the objective and the eyepiece are converging lenses.
(c) In a compound microscope, the objective forms a real, inverted and magnified image of the object.
(d) The final image formed by an astronomical refracting telescope is erect.
(e) In the normal adjustment of an astronomical telescope, the final image is formed at infinity.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Compound microscope and astronomical telescope
solution.explanation: A telescope needs f_o ≫ f_e for large magnification (m = f_o/f_e), and its final image is inverted. In a microscope, two converging lenses are used; the objective forms a real, inverted, magnified intermediate image that the eyepiece magnifies further.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (a) or (d) include a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A travelling microscope is focused on a mark on a table. A glass slab 6 cm thick, of refractive index 1.5, is then placed over the mark. To bring the mark back into focus, the microscope must be raised through:

solution.concept: Normal shift due to a slab: s = t(1 − 1/n)
solution.explanation: Seen through the slab, the mark appears raised by t(1 − 1/n), because the slab's thickness t appears as only t/n. The microscope must be raised by this apparent shift.
steps: Apparent thickness of the slab = t/n = 6/1.5 = 4 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 cm is the apparent thickness t/n, not the shift. 9 cm multiplies by n. 3 cm uses t(n − 1).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction (real and apparent depth)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A convex lens forms a real image, three times the size of the object, on a screen placed 80 cm from the object. The focal length of the lens is:

solution.concept: Lens formula with magnification for a real image: v = 3|u| and |u| + v = object–screen distance
solution.explanation: For a real image formed on a screen, object and image lie on opposite sides of the lens, so the distances add.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 cm comes from treating the image as virtual (v − |u| = 80), which cannot be caught on a screen. 20 cm is the object distance. 30 cm takes f = v/2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', thin lens formula; magnification

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment the two slits give waves of equal intensity, and the maximum intensity on the screen is I_max. At a point on the screen where the path difference between the two waves is λ/3, the intensity is:

solution.concept: Resultant intensity of two coherent waves: I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2), with φ = (2π/λ) × path difference
solution.explanation: With equal intensities I₀, the maximum is 4I₀, so I = I_max cos²(φ/2).
solution.why_others_wrong: 3I_max/4 uses φ = π/3 (cos²(π/6)), i.e. forgets the factor 2π. I_max/2 is the result for a path difference of λ/4. I_max/3 assumes the intensity falls in proportion to the path difference.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', coherent and incoherent addition of waves

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A prism has a refracting angle of 60°. Light falls on one refracting face. For no light to emerge from the second refracting face, whatever the angle of incidence on the first face, the refractive index of the prism material must be at least:

solution.concept: Refraction through a prism: r₁ + r₂ = A, with r₁ at most equal to the critical angle C
solution.explanation: The largest possible r₁ (grazing incidence) is C, which makes r₂ = A − C as small as possible. If even this smallest r₂ is not less than C, every ray is totally reflected at the second face. So the condition is A − C ≥ C, i.e. A ≥ 2C.
steps: No emergence for any i: A − C ≥ C → C ≤ A/2 = 30°
solution.why_others_wrong: √2 corresponds to C = 45°, the limiting value for a 90° prism. 2/√3 corresponds to C = 60°, using A ≥ C instead of A ≥ 2C. 1.5 is just a typical value for glass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism; total internal reflection

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 2 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm, placed 25 cm apart. The microscope is adjusted so that the final image is at infinity. Taking the least distance of distinct vision as 25 cm, the magnifying power of the microscope is:

solution.concept: Compound microscope: m = m_o × m_e, with m_e = D/f_e for a final image at infinity
solution.explanation: For the final image at infinity, the objective's image must be at the focus of the eyepiece, which fixes v_o. The lens formula then gives u_o and the objective magnification.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 uses the approximation (L/f_o)(D/f_e) with L = 20 cm, and 62.5 the same with L = 25 cm; neither is exact here. 54 uses m_e = 1 + D/f_e, which applies when the final image is at the near point.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', the compound microscope

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Diffraction of light is easily observed around everyday objects such as doors and windows.
Reason (R): Diffraction effects become noticeable when the size of the obstacle or aperture is comparable to the wavelength of the wave.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: When diffraction is noticeable
solution.explanation: The wavelength of visible light (about 0.4–0.7 µm) is tiny compared with doors and windows, so the bending of light round them is negligible and they cast sharp shadows. Diffraction of light becomes noticeable only with very small apertures or obstacles. A is false; R is true.
steps: Door width ~ 1 m ≫ λ of light → negligible diffraction → A false
R is the condition for marked diffraction → true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C are wrong. (Sound, of wavelength ~ 1 m, does bend round doors — which is why A sounds plausible.)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In an interference pattern, light energy is not destroyed at the dark fringes; it is redistributed, the intensity being greater than the sum of the separate intensities at the bright fringes.
Statement II: The first minimum of a single-slit diffraction pattern occurs where a sin θ = λ, which can be understood by dividing the slit into two halves whose corresponding points send waves with a path difference of λ/2.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
